title: LEAD: Length-Efficient Adaptive and Dynamic Reasoning for Large Language Models
claim: A multi-stage procedure adaptively calibrates per-problem target lengths and dynamically weights correctness and efficiency rewards to produce one combined advantage.
layout: 4 panels, left-to-right, numbered circles, worked numeric example flowing through stages
description: A four-stage left-to-right pipeline with numbered dark circles. Panel 1 (gray) shows sampling G rollouts for a prompt, listing lengths such as 1800, 2600, 1400, 3700 and 1200 tokens with green check or red cross marks for correctness. Panel 2 (blue frame) filters the correct rollouts, computes their mean length of 1867 as the target L*, and draws a number line of efficiency reward. The reward peaks at 1 at the target and falls linearly to -1 on either side. Panel 3 (blue frame) shows a grid of five rollouts with green and red boxes. Rows give lengths, correctness rewards, efficiency rewards and the two separate advantages. Below the grid is a small PSI controller line plot of the two weights over training. Panel 4 (gray) holds the equations that combine the advantages and batch-whiten them. Blue frames mark the contributions and gray frames mark the GRPO components. The eye goes first to the numbered boxes and the green/red values.
caption: LEAD framework. (1) Sample $G$ rollouts per prompt $q$ from the old policy $\pi_{\theta_old}$ and score each by correctness $r_c$. (2) Per-problem online target-length calibration: filter to correct rollouts $\mathcal{C}_q$, set $L^*_q$ to their mean, and compute the symmetric efficiency reward $r_\ell$, which peaks at $\ell{=}L^*_q$ and decays linearly to $-1$ on either side. (3) Dynamic reward weighting: each reward is group-normalized separately to produce decoupled advantages $A^{(c)}_{q,j}$ and $A^{(\ell)}_{q,j}$, and the PSI controller adapts the weights $(\lambda_c^{(t)}, \lambda_\ell^{(t)})$ online from per-reward instability and headroom. (4) The two advantage channels are linearly combined under the EMA-smoothed weights and batch-whitened to obtain the effective advantage $A_{q,j}$ used in the GRPO objective. \textcolor[RGB]{0,155,230}{Blue-framed} components are LEAD's contributions; gray-framed components are inherited from GRPO.
abstract: Large reasoning models, such as OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek-R1, tend to become increasingly verbose as their reasoning capabilities improve. These inflated Chain-of-Thought (CoT) trajectories often exceed what the underlying problems require, wasting compute, latency, and context budgets. While introducing length-based efficiency rewards during reinforcement learning offers a natural remedy, existing methods struggle with two fundamental challenges: the optimal balance between correctness and efficiency is non-stationary throughout training, and intrinsic reasoning budgets vary drastically across problems. Relying on static reward weights and global length constraints inevitably forces a compromise between degraded accuracy and unrealized compression. To overcome these limitations, we propose LEAD (Length-Efficient Adaptive and Dynamic reasoning), a method that replaces static heuristics with online, self-adaptive mechanisms. LEAD dynamically calibrates the correctness--efficiency trade-off at each step using a Potential-Scaled Instability, directing optimization capacity to the most informative learning signal. Furthermore, it estimates an adaptive per-problem target length online based on the model's own correct rollouts, applying a symmetric efficiency reward that penalizes both overthinking and over-compression. Evaluated on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, LEAD achieves the highest accuracy and Accuracy-Efficiency Score among RL-trained efficient-reasoning methods in our matched comparisons while producing substantially shorter outputs than the base model.
